name: Paneer Paratha
equipment: Flat tawa or heavy non-stick pan
Mixing bowl and a second small bowl for the filling
Small spoon and a flat spatula (palta)
Kitchen scale and measuring spoons (or use the household measures)

steps.title: Mix the dough ingredients
steps.text: In a bowl put 50 g atta, 0.3 g salt (a small pinch) and 0.2 g ajwain (a small pinch). Mix with your fingers.
steps.visualCue: An even, pale-brown, loose flour with no white salt streaks
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl of flour with the pinch of ajwain
steps.watchOut: Ajwain clumping in one spot, which gives bitter bites; rub the pinch between your palms as you add it so it spreads.

steps.title: Add water slowly
steps.text: Pour 25 ml water (about 2 tbsp) into the flour, mixing as you go, then add up to 5 ml more only if crumbs will not come together.
steps.visualCue: Shaggy lumps that start to stick together into one rough mass
steps.cameraCheck: The rough dough in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Water poured slowly into flour while a hand mixes
steps.watchOut: Pouring all the water at once: a sticky dough clings to your hands and the board. Rescue by dusting in 1 tsp flour at a time.

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Press, fold and push the dough with the heel of your hand for 3 min.
steps.visualCue: Soft, smooth, springs back slowly when you press a finger in, and no longer sticks to your hand
steps.cameraCheck: The smooth dough ball on the board
steps.videoShot: Hands kneading with the heel of the palm
steps.watchOut: A stiff, cracked dough (too little water or too little kneading), which tears when stuffed. Wet your hand and knead 1 min more.

steps.title: Rest the dough
steps.text: Cover the bowl with a damp cloth or lid and leave it for 20 min.
steps.tip: Make the filling during this rest.
steps.visualCue: The dough feels softer and more stretchy when pressed
steps.videoShot: A damp cloth being laid over the bowl
steps.watchOut: Skipping the rest or leaving it uncovered: the dough shrinks back when rolled and dries into a crust. Cover it; a dry skin can be kneaded in with a few drops of water.

steps.title: Crumble the paneer
steps.text: Grate or crumble 40 g paneer into a small bowl.
steps.visualCue: Fine, even crumbs with no big lumps
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl of fine paneer crumbs
steps.watchOut: Big lumps, which poke through the dough when rolled. Mash any lumps flat with the back of a fork.

steps.title: Prepare the flavourings
steps.text: Finely chop ½ small green chilli (3 g) and 1 tbsp coriander (3 g), and grate ½-inch ginger (2 g).
steps.cameraCheck: The three prepared items on a plate
steps.watchOut: Big chilli or ginger pieces, which tear the dough and give hot bites. Chop them to the size of rice grains.

steps.title: Make the filling
steps.text: Add the chilli, coriander and ginger to the paneer with ¼ tsp amchur, a pinch each of garam masala, red chilli powder and cumin powder, and 0.4 g salt (a small pinch). Mix lightly.
steps.visualCue: A speckled, crumbly mixture that holds together when pressed in your hand
steps.cameraCheck: The mixed filling in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Spices sprinkled over paneer and mixed
steps.watchOut: Adding water or curd to the filling: wet filling makes the paratha tear and stick. If it is damp, mix in 1 tsp dry atta to soak it up.

steps.title: Shape the dough into a ball
steps.text: Knead the rested dough for 20 sec and roll it into a smooth ball between your palms.
steps.visualCue: A smooth ball with no cracks, about the size of a lime
steps.cameraCheck: The dough ball in your palm
steps.videoShot: A ball being rolled between two palms
steps.watchOut: A cracked ball: filling leaks from the cracks later. Wet your fingers lightly and smooth the cracks closed.

steps.title: Roll out a small circle
steps.text: Dip the ball in the 5 g dry atta, then roll it into a circle about 9 cm wide, thicker in the middle.
steps.visualCue: A flat, round disc about the size of a small bowl's mouth
steps.cameraCheck: The small rolled disc on the board
steps.videoShot: A rolling pin shaping a small disc
steps.watchOut: Rolling too thin: a very thin disc tears when stuffed. Roll only to about 3 mm.

steps.title: Add the filling
steps.text: Put all the filling in the centre of the disc and spread it lightly, leaving a 1 cm edge clear.
steps.visualCue: A mound of speckled filling with a clean dough rim
steps.cameraCheck: The disc with filling in the centre
steps.videoShot: A spoon placing filling on the disc
steps.watchOut: Filling on the rim: it stops the edge sticking and the paratha opens up in the pan. Wipe any filling off the rim with your fingertip.

steps.title: Seal the paratha
steps.text: Lift the edge of the disc all around and pinch it together over the filling, like a bundle, then twist off the top.
steps.tip: Turn the pouch seam-side down before rolling.
steps.visualCue: A closed round pouch with the seam on top and no filling showing
steps.cameraCheck: The closed pouch, seam side up
steps.videoShot: Edges pinched together over the filling
steps.watchOut: A gap in the seam: filling bursts out when rolled. Pinch the seam again and press it shut firmly.

steps.title: Flatten the pouch
steps.text: Press the pouch flat between your palms (seam side down), dip it in dry atta, and set it on the board.
steps.visualCue: A flat, thick round with a dusting of flour on both faces
steps.cameraCheck: The flattened pouch on the board
steps.videoShot: A palm pressing the pouch flat
steps.watchOut: Skipping the dusting: the paratha sticks to the board and tears. Dust both sides lightly.

steps.title: Roll the paratha
steps.text: Roll gently with light pressure into a round about 15 cm wide, turning it a quarter turn after each roll.
steps.tip: Roll from the centre outward, not back and forth.
steps.visualCue: An even round, with the filling visible as a faint shadow, and no filling showing through
steps.videoShot: Rolling pin turning the paratha a quarter turn at a time
steps.watchOut: Pressing hard: the filling pushes through and the paratha tears. If it tears, patch the hole with a pinch of dough and dust it. Roll lightly from the centre outward.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Heat the tawa on medium-high for 1–2 min.
steps.visualCue: A drop of water sizzles and vanishes within 2 seconds
steps.cameraCheck: A water drop sizzling on the tawa
steps.videoShot: A water drop dancing on a hot tawa
steps.watchOut: A cold tawa: the paratha turns pale, hard and chewy. A smoking tawa burns it; lower the flame if it smokes.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Place the paratha on the tawa and cook for 30–40 sec.
steps.visualCue: Small bubbles rise, the dough turns from raw white to slightly opaque with pale spots
steps.cameraCheck: The paratha on the tawa with bubbles
steps.videoShot: A paratha on the tawa with small bubbles forming
steps.watchOut: Waiting for brown spots on side one: it dries out and cannot puff. Flip as soon as it is opaque with a few pale spots.

steps.title: Flip and add ghee
steps.text: Flip the paratha, cook 30 sec, then spread ½ tsp (2.5 g) ghee on top.
steps.visualCue: The ghee melts and sizzles, with brown spots starting under the paratha
steps.cameraCheck: The paratha with ghee melting on top
steps.videoShot: Ghee spread over the paratha with a spoon
steps.watchOut: Too much ghee at once: it pools, and the filling can spit out. Use only ½ tsp per side.

steps.title: Flip again and finish
steps.text: Flip the paratha, spread the other ½ tsp (2.5 g) ghee, and press gently with the spatula, moving it around for 30–40 sec until golden.
steps.visualCue: Golden-brown spots all over, a nutty smell, and the paratha puffs slightly
steps.cameraCheck: Both sides of the golden paratha
steps.videoShot: Spatula pressing the golden paratha edges
steps.watchOut: Pressing hard on the middle: the filling squeezes out. Press around the edges, not the centre. Black spots and a burnt smell mean the flame is too high.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Transfer to a plate and serve hot with curd, pickle or white butter.
steps.visualCue: Steam rises and the filling is hot through when you break it open
steps.cameraCheck: The paratha on a plate with curd or pickle
steps.videoShot: A paratha torn open to show the steaming filling
steps.watchOut: Stacking hot parathas tightly: they turn soggy. Keep them side by side or wrapped loosely in a cloth.

reasons: whole wheat dough gives about 6 g fibre, the paratha has a useful 13.6 g protein from paneer, no frying in deep oil, and only 0.7 g salt. Points off for about 8.8 g saturated fat from paneer and ghee, and it is a dense, calorie-rich bread. Restaurant versions usually add butter or ghee generously, use a thicker stuffing with cheese or onion, and cost more in oil, so the plate is heavier and higher in saturated fat and sodium (est.).

researchRating.basis: one of the most widely published and loved stuffed parathas in India; nearly every major recipe site and blog carries it (Hebbar's Kitchen, Swasthi, Cookclickndevour, Jeyashri's Kitchen, Sanjeev Kapoor, Cook with Kushi, Swiggy Instamart), usually described as a quick, filling breakfast or lunchbox item. Points off because the recipe pages could not be opened here, so vote counts and star averages could not be read, and because sources note the filling can tear or dry out.

storage: Best eaten fresh. Fridge-safe in a closed box for up to 1 day (cool within 1 hour; paneer is a perishable filling). Freezing cooked parathas is possible for about 1 month, but the texture suffers (est.). Reheat on a tawa on medium for 1 min per side, not in the microwave, which makes it chewy.
leftoverRemix: Paneer paratha roll. Spread 1 tbsp green chutney on a cold leftover paratha, add thin slices of cucumber and tomato and a pinch of chaat masala, and roll it up tightly in foil or paper.
burnOff: about 5.0 km of running (350 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 7.0 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 24 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: wheat flour is a grain, so use kuttu (buckwheat) or singhare (water chestnut) flour with 1 boiled mashed potato to bind and sendha (rock) salt; skip ajwain and garam masala if your family does. Assumption: the common rule set (no grains, table salt), which differs by family.

ekadashi.reason: whole wheat is a grain, which the common rule set avoids on Ekadashi. (A kuttu or singhare version may be accepted in some families; not confirmed.)

jain.reason: drop the fresh ginger and use dry ginger powder (sonth) and hing; the rest (wheat, paneer, chilli, coriander, spices) has no onion, garlic or root vegetable.

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; filling, with about 13.6 g protein and 6 g fibre per paratha, and moderate salt (about 290 mg sodium). Serve with curd for a fuller sehri.

jain.reason: the main recipe uses fresh ginger (a root); swap it for dry ginger powder (sonth) and add a pinch of hing. Paneer is dairy and is allowed.

vegan.reason: paneer and ghee are dairy. See the Vegan variant (tofu paratha).

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, so it fits a pescatarian diet.

sattvik.reason: the recipe uses no onion, garlic or hing. (Many restaurant versions add onion, so check when ordering.)

glutenFree.reason: whole wheat flour (atta) dough. Not researched yet for a gluten-free version.

dairyFree.reason: paneer and ghee. See the Dairy-free variant (same as the tofu paratha).
